content.title: Identifying Independent and Subordinate Clauses
content.overview: Mastering the ACT English section requires the ability to distinguish between independent and subordinate (dependent) clauses. This skill is the foundation for fixing fragments, run-ons, and punctuation errors.
learning_objectives: Identify the components of an independent clause: subject, verb, and complete thought.
Recognize subordinate clauses by identifying subordinating conjunctions and relative pronouns.
Apply the Clause-Role Tagging strategy to determine how clauses should be punctuated.

sections.title: The Independent Clause
sections.content: An independent clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought. It is grammatically self-sufficient, meaning it can stand alone as a complete sentence. For example, in the sentence 'The scientist analyzed the data,' 'The scientist' is the subject and 'analyzed' is the verb. The thought is complete, so this is an independent clause.

sections.title: The Subordinate (Dependent) Clause
sections.content: A subordinate clause also contains a subject and a verb, but it does not express a complete thought. It 'depends' on an independent clause to make sense. These clauses typically begin with subordinating conjunctions (e.g., because, although, since, if, when, while) or relative pronouns (e.g., who, which, that). For example, 'Because the scientist analyzed the data' is a subordinate clause; the word 'because' creates a need for more information, preventing it from being a complete sentence.

sections.title: The Clause-Role Tagging Strategy
sections.content: When you encounter an underlined clause on the ACT, use these steps: 1. Check for a subject and a main verb. 2. Determine if the thought is complete or if it starts with a subordinating word. 3. Tag the clause as INDEPENDENT (IND) or SUBORDINATE (SUB). 4. Apply punctuation rules: IND + IND requires a semicolon or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). SUB + IND requires a comma after the subordinate clause. IND + SUB usually requires no comma unless the subordinate clause is non-essential (nonrestrictive).

worked_examples.question: Identify the clause type and correct punctuation for: 'Although the rain stopped the game did not resume.'
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Analyze 'Although the rain stopped.' It has a subject (rain) and verb (stopped) but starts with the subordinating conjunction 'Although.' Tag: SUBORDINATE. Step 2: Analyze 'the game did not resume.' It has a subject (game) and verb (did resume) and is a complete thought. Tag: INDEPENDENT. Step 3: Apply the rule for SUB + IND. A comma must follow the subordinate clause. Corrected: 'Although the rain stopped, the game did not resume.'

worked_examples.question: Choose the correct version: 'The new software rolled out on Monday (which the support team expected).'
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Tag the first clause 'The new software rolled out on Monday.' It is INDEPENDENT. Step 2: Tag the second clause 'which the support team expected.' It starts with the relative pronoun 'which' and cannot stand alone. Tag: SUBORDINATE. Step 3: Since 'which' introduces non-essential information about the rollout, it must be preceded by a comma. Corrected: 'The new software rolled out on Monday, which the support team expected.'

common_mistakes: Treating a subordinate clause as a complete sentence (creating a fragment).
Mistaking a relative pronoun (like 'which') for a subject that can start an independent clause.
Forgetting that a clause starting with 'because' or 'although' is dependent even if it has a subject and a verb.
exam_tips: If a clause starts with a 'W' word (who, which, where, when) or 'that,' it is almost always a subordinate clause.
Read the clause in isolation. If it sounds like it's 'hanging' or waiting for more information, it is subordinate.
Watch out for 'FANBOYS' (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). These join two independent clauses, they do not make a clause subordinate.
content.recap: Independent clauses can stand alone as sentences; subordinate clauses cannot because they begin with subordinating words. Use the Clause-Role Tagging strategy to identify these components and ensure they are joined by the correct punctuation.

knowledge_claims.content: An independent clause must contain a subject, a verb, and express a complete thought.
A subordinate clause contains a subject and a verb but begins with a subordinating word that prevents it from expressing a complete thought.
Words like 'because,' 'although,' 'since,' 'if,' and 'while' are subordinating conjunctions that signal a subordinate clause.
Relative pronouns such as 'who,' 'which,' and 'that' typically introduce subordinate clauses.
The Clause-Role Tagging strategy involves checking for a subject/verb, identifying subordinating words, and tagging the clause as INDEPENDENT or SUBORDINATE.
When a sentence begins with a subordinate clause followed by an independent clause, a comma must separate them.
Two independent clauses cannot be joined by only a comma; they require a semicolon or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction.
A clause that starts with 'which' is usually a nonrestrictive subordinate clause and requires a comma before it when it follows an independent clause.
It is a mistake to assume a clause is independent just because it has a subject and a verb; the presence of a subordinating conjunction makes it dependent.
To verify if a clause is independent, read it alone to see if it functions as a grammatically complete sentence.
Unlike independent clauses, subordinate clauses function as modifiers (adjectives or adverbs) or nouns within a larger sentence structure.
In the sentence 'If it rains, we will stay inside,' 'If it rains' is tagged as SUBORDINATE and 'we will stay inside' is tagged as INDEPENDENT.

items.stem:
Practice form 1. Rina is editing a short report about a community garden.

Which option is an independent clause?
A) The volunteers completed the survey.
B) Because the volunteers completed the survey
C) Although the survey was complete
D) When the volunteers arrived

options.B: Because the volunteers completed the survey

items.explanation: The correct choice directly applies the target skill: 识别独立分句与从属分句.

videoLesson.title: Identify Independent and Subordinate Clauses
videoLesson.description: Recognize whether a highlighted clause has its own subject, main verb, and a complete thought. Tag clauses INDEPENDENT or SUBORDINATE and select punctuation that preserves the main clause.
